title: Elementary Idea of the Quantum Mechanical Model — de Broglie's Wave Equation
topicTitle: Elementary idea of quantum mechanical model: de Broglie's wave equation
notes: ### 1. Meaning — dual nature of matter

Light behaves both as a wave and as a stream of particles (photons). In 1924 Louis de Broglie proposed the converse for matter: every moving material particle has a wave associated with it. These waves are called **matter waves** or de Broglie waves, and the hypothesis is the bridge from Bohr's orbits to the quantum-mechanical model.
### 2. de Broglie's wave equation

For a particle of mass m moving with speed v, wavelength $\lambda=\frac{h}{mv}=\frac{h}{p}$; using kinetic energy, $\lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2mKE}}$; for an electron accelerated through a potential difference V volts, $\lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}=\sqrt{\frac{150}{V}}\ \text{Å}\approx\frac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}}\ \text{Å}$. Derivation sketch: from $E=mc^{2}$ and $E=h\nu$ for a photon, $\lambda=h/p$ is obtained and applied to matter.
### 3. Meaning of the numbers

λ ∝ 1/m and ∝ 1/v: a 1 g mass moving at 1 m s⁻¹ has λ ≈ 6.6 × 10⁻³¹ m — unobservably small, which is why cricket balls show no wave nature. A 100 V electron has λ ≈ 1.23 Å, comparable with atomic spacings, so crystals diffract electrons. Wave behaviour is therefore a *microscopic* phenomenon.
### 4. Experimental proof

Davisson and Germer (1927) diffracted slow electrons from a nickel crystal and obtained a diffraction pattern whose maxima obey nλ = d sin θ; G. P. Thomson obtained similar patterns with high-speed electrons. Electron diffraction is the direct proof of matter waves.
### 5. How de Broglie's idea repairs Bohr's model

If the electron forms a standing wave round the orbit, the circumference must contain a whole number of wavelengths: nλ = 2πr. Substituting λ = h/mv gives mvr = nh/2π — Bohr's *unexplained* quantisation postulate now has a physical meaning. Modern quantum mechanics (Schrödinger, 1926) replaced the orbit by a wave function ψ, whose square |ψ|² gives the probability density of finding the electron — the **orbital**.
### 6. Applications
• Electron microscopes use the tiny λ of accelerated electrons to resolve objects far smaller than light allows; electron and neutron diffraction determine crystal and molecular structures.
• Explains quantisation of energy levels, the origin of quantum numbers, quantum tunnelling (STM, tunnel diodes, alpha decay) and the whole wave-mechanical picture of the atom.
• Underlies semiconductor physics, quantum dots, lasers and matter-wave interferometry (atom interferometers, BEC experiments).
### 7. Limitations of the elementary treatment

λ = h/mv is non-relativistic (for v close to c use λ = h/√(p² + (mv)²/c²) type corrections); the wave function is a *probability amplitude*, not a mechanical wave in a medium; the simple equation applies to a single free particle and needs the Schrödinger equation in a potential; the wavelength of everyday objects is far too small to detect.
### Focus of this tab
The derivation of λ = h/mv from the photon equations and the experimental proof — the two parts of de Broglie's idea that complete the main note.
### Derivation from the photon picture

For a photon: $E=h\nu$ and $E=mc^{2}$ (equivalence of energy and mass). Equating: $mc^{2}=h\nu=h\frac{c}{\lambda}$ → $\lambda=\frac{h}{mc}=\frac{h}{p}$. de Broglie's 1924 leap: the same relation must hold for **matter**, so a particle of momentum p = mv has wavelength $\lambda=\frac{h}{mv}$. For accelerated electrons, $\lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}=\frac{12.27}{\sqrt{V}}\ \text{Å}$ (V in volts).
### Why the wave nature is only microscopic

λ ∝ 1/m: a 1 g body at 1 m s⁻¹ has λ ≈ 6.6 × 10⁻³¹ m (undetectable), while a 100 V electron has λ ≈ 1.23 Å — the size of atomic spacings, so crystals diffract electrons. Wave behaviour is not absent for large bodies; it is unobservable.
### Experimental proof (Davisson–Germer, 1927)

Electrons accelerated through ≈54 V strike a single nickel crystal; the detector records a maximum at φ = 50°. Bragg's law gives the wavelength: nλ = 2d sin θ with d = 0.091 nm → λ ≈ 0.165 nm; the de Broglie value for 54 V is λ = 12.27/√54 ≈ 1.67 Å = 0.167 nm — agreement within experiment. G. P. Thomson's high-energy electron diffraction through thin films confirmed it independently (both shared the 1937 Nobel Prize).
### Consequences that matter for chemistry
• Justifies Bohr's quantisation: nλ = 2πr → mvr = nh/2π.
• Basis of the Schrödinger equation and the orbital concept.
• Electron diffraction and the electron microscope (λ ≈ 0.005 nm at 50 kV → atomic resolution); neutron diffraction for structure determination.
• Quantum tunnelling and matter-wave interferometry (atom interferometers, BEC) are direct technologies of matter waves.
The equation that turned de Broglie's matter waves into the quantum-mechanical model — what ψ means, what solving it gives, and how the four quantum numbers appear.
### The equation (elementary form)

For a particle moving in one dimension: $-\frac{h^{2}}{8\pi^{2}m}\frac{d^{2}\psi}{dx^{2}}+V\psi=E\psi$, i.e. $\hat{H}\psi=E\psi$ — a wave equation in which the 'wave property' comes from de Broglie (through the momentum operator) and the energy from classical mechanics. For the hydrogen atom V is the Coulomb potential, and the equation is solved in spherical coordinates $(r,\theta,\phi)$.
### What ψ and ψ² mean

ψ itself has no direct physical meaning; the measurable quantity is **|ψ|², the probability density** — the chance of finding the electron in a unit volume at that point. Max Born supplied this interpretation. The total probability over all space is normalised to 1 (∫|ψ|²dV = 1). Regions where ψ = 0 are **nodes**.
### What solving the hydrogen atom gives

• A set of allowed wave functions ψₙ,ₗ,ₘ (orbitals) labelled by three quantum numbers — n (size/energy), l (shape), m (orientation) — that arise automatically from the boundary conditions (ψ must be single-valued, finite and vanish at infinity).
• Energies $E_{n}=-13.6/n^{2}$ eV, agreeing with Bohr — but degeneracy appears: for n = 2 the solutions 2s and 2p have the same energy, which Bohr cannot give.
• Probability distributions instead of paths: the electron cloud, radial probability maxima (0.529 Å for 1s), and orbital shapes (spherical s, dumbbell p).
### Why this replaces Bohr

The uncertainty principle forbids definite orbits; Schrödinger's equation never uses a trajectory. It works for multi-electron atoms (approximately, with effective nuclear charge), explains fine structure when spin is added, and predicts molecular bonding — every defect of Bohr's theory is repaired.
confusion: ❌ Matter waves are electromagnetic waves. ✅ They are probability (matter) waves carrying no charge; they are not E–B oscillations.
❌ Heavier bodies have longer wavelengths. ✅ λ = h/mv — larger mass means a *shorter* (unobservable) wavelength.
❌ de Broglie's hypothesis was accepted immediately on publication. ✅ It became convincing only after the Davisson–Germer electron-diffraction experiment (1927).
❌ de Broglie's waves replace Bohr's quantisation with nothing. ✅ They *justify* it through the standing-wave condition nλ = 2πr.
❌ An electron microscope uses electron particles and light waves together. ✅ It uses the electron's short de Broglie wavelength, not visible light.
❌ de Broglie waves travel at the speed of light. ✅ They travel with the particle (v ≪ c); the phase velocity even exceeds c, while the group velocity equals v.
❌ The derivation needs relativistic mass. ✅ For non-relativistic particles λ = h/mv directly; the photon derivation only motivates the form.
❌ Davisson–Germer proved light has particle nature. ✅ It proved *electrons* have wave nature — the converse of the photoelectric effect.
❌ ψ is a measurable wave like a light wave. ✅ ψ is a probability amplitude; only |ψ|² is physically meaningful.
❌ Quantum numbers are put in by hand. ✅ They emerge from solving the equation with boundary conditions.
❌ Solving the equation gives exact paths. ✅ It gives probability distributions; trajectories do not exist.

universalFacts: de Broglie proposed matter waves in his 1924 PhD thesis and won the 1929 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Davisson and Germer confirmed electron diffraction in 1927 (Nobel Prize 1937).
λ for a 100 V electron ≈ 1.23 Å; a 1 g body at 1 m s⁻¹ has λ ≈ 6.6 × 10⁻³¹ m — undetectable.
answer pattern for "Elementary idea of quantum mechanical model: de Broglie's…": define → method → result. Structure earns the marks on 6–10 mark questions.
de Broglie received the 1929 Nobel Prize for his 1924 thesis — the first Nobel awarded for a PhD thesis.
λ(54 V electron) ≈ 1.67 Å matched the Davisson–Germer Bragg analysis (d = 0.091 nm, φ = 50°).
Electron microscopes reach ≈0.1 nm resolution because λ(electron) is ~10⁵ times shorter than visible light.
Schrödinger published the equation in 1926 and received the Nobel Prize in 1933 (shared with Dirac).
The hydrogen solution reproduces Bohr's −13.6/n² eV energies exactly, plus the degeneracy Bohr missed.
The name 'orbital' replaced 'orbit' because ψ² gives a probability cloud, not a path.
examples: **Problem:** de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving at 10⁶ m s⁻¹. **Solution:** λ = 6.626×10⁻³⁴/(9.11×10⁻³¹ × 10⁶) = 7.27 × 10⁻¹⁰ m = 0.727 nm.

**Problem:** Wavelength of a 1.0 g bullet moving at 300 m s⁻¹. **Solution:** λ = 6.626×10⁻³⁴/(10⁻³ × 300) = 2.2 × 10⁻³³ m — many orders of magnitude smaller than any aperture, so no diffraction is observed.

**Problem:** λ of an electron with KE = 13.6 eV. **Solution:** λ = 12.27/√13.6 ≈ 3.33 Å — exactly one circumference of the first Bohr orbit, linking the two topics.

**Problem:** Why does the equation give discrete energies? **Solution:** acceptable ψ must be continuous, single-valued and normalisable; these boundary conditions are satisfied only for special values of E — the same logic that quantises a vibrating guitar string.
